item.title: Seto Inland Sea Seafood: Tai and Shirasu — Guide
item.description: The Seto Inland Sea that laps Kagawa’s coast is a calm, sheltered, nutrient-rich body of water that produces some of Japan’s finest seafood. Its star is tai, sea bream — firm, sweet, elegant white fish long considered auspicious and served as sashimi, grilled, simmered, or in rice dishes, and especially prized here in spring. Alongside it, Kagawa’s waters yield shirasu (tiny translucent whitebait, eaten fresh or lightly boiled over rice), hamachi and buri yellowtail (much of it farmed in the region), octopus, and a variety of shellfish.

item.title: Taimeshi: Ehime's Sea Bream Rice — Guide
item.description: Sea bream (tai) is the pride of Ehime’s seas, and taimeshi — sea bream rice — is the prefecture’s signature dish, uniquely served in two quite different regional styles. In the Matsuyama and central area, taimeshi means a whole sea bream baked or simmered with rice in a pot, its savoury flavour infusing the grains, then flaked and mixed through. In the southern Uwajima region, taimeshi is completely different: fresh raw sea bream sashimi in a rich sauce of soy, egg and sesame, poured over hot rice — a bold, glossy donburi.

item.title: Akashi Sea Bream: Japan's Most Prized Tai — Guide
item.description: Akashi-dai, the sea bream caught in the strait between Kobe and Awaji Island, is regarded as the finest in Japan and priced accordingly. The reason is the water: the Akashi Strait funnels enormous tidal flows between the Inland Sea and Osaka Bay, and fish that spend their lives swimming against that current develop dense, firm, well-muscled flesh with a clean sweetness. Restaurants around Akashi serve it every way — sashimi cut thin enough to see the plate through, salt-grilled whole, simmered with soy, and as tai-meshi, rice cooked with the fish and its broth.
